learn.hook: She cooks, irons, waits on everyone and is thanked by no one. Then her neighbour suggests a magic trick that will change everything.
points: J.B. Priestley was an English novelist and dramatist; 'Mother's Day' is a one-act comic play.
Setting: the living room of the Pearson family's house, on an afternoon in early autumn.
Mrs Annie Pearson is taken for granted by her husband George, her daughter Doris and her son Cyril.
She is meek and self-sacrificing: she runs after them, irons their clothes and waits up for them, but never complains to their faces.
The play will show her learning to be firm.

steps: She works hard for her family.

She is too meek to stand up for herself.
example.answer: Her family treats her as a servant, and she is too gentle to assert herself.

learn.reallife: National surveys in India show women spend several hours a day on unpaid household work. Priestley's play, written decades ago, still feels current.

topics.title: Mrs Fitzgerald and the Eastern spell

learn.hook: Enter the neighbour: a bold Irish fortune-teller who smokes, speaks her mind, and knows a spell from her years in the East.
points: Mrs Fitzgerald, the neighbour, is a bold, confident Irish fortune-teller who urges Mrs Pearson to assert herself and be the boss.
Mrs Pearson is too timid to do it; so Mrs Fitzgerald suggests they swap personalities using a spell she learnt in the East.
They hold hands, she murmurs the spell, and their personalities exchange bodies: a fantasy body swap.
Mrs Fitzgerald is the catalyst: the person who triggers change.
Devices: fantasy (body swap), dramatic irony (the audience knows of the swap, the family does not) and slapstick humour.

example.q: What is dramatic irony in this play?
steps: The audience knows the two women have swapped.
So we laugh as they react to 'Mother's' strange behaviour.
example.answer: The audience knows Mrs Fitzgerald is inside Mrs Pearson's body while the family doesn't: that gap creates dramatic irony.

learn.reallife: Indian films like 'Chaalbaaz' or TV comedies use swapped identities for laughs. Priestley's play uses the same fantasy trick.

topics.title: Mrs Fitzgerald in charge: the family is shocked

learn.hook: Imagine coming home and your gentle mother is smoking, drinking stout, playing cards and refusing to make tea. Welcome to the Pearson household.
points: Mrs Fitzgerald, now in Mrs Pearson's body, smokes, drinks stout and refuses to serve the family.
She mocks Doris's date with Charlie Spence and refuses to iron her clothes; she rebukes Cyril for his careless demands.
She shocks George by telling him people at the club laugh at him behind his back and call him 'Pompy-ompy Pearson'.
The family is stunned; they begin to apologise and offer help.
George: self-important; Doris: selfish; Cyril: careless and demanding.

example.q: How does 'Mrs Pearson' (Mrs Fitzgerald inside) treat George?
steps: She tells him the club members laugh at him.
example.answer: She shocks his pride by revealing that people laugh at him and mock him with a nickname.

learn.reallife: Many Indian homes saw the same shift when a mother went on 'strike' for a day: suddenly everyone noticed how much she did.

topics.title: Swapping back: the real Mrs Pearson takes charge

learn.hook: The magic wears off and the real Mrs Pearson is back. The question is: has she learnt anything?
points: The two women swap back; the real Mrs Pearson returns to her own body.
Mrs Fitzgerald warns her not to go soft; Mrs Pearson now firmly sets the terms.
Ending: the family agrees to stay at home, play a game of rummy and help with supper, while Mrs Pearson and George have a talk.
Role reversal brings change: the family sees what it is like to be treated as they treated her.
Is the solution realistic? The magic is fantasy, but the lesson (being firm earns respect) is realistic. One-act structure, stage directions and comic dialogue keep it brisk.

example.q: How does the role reversal bring change?
steps: The family is treated the way they treated her.
When she returns, she uses this to set firm terms.
example.answer: By being treated harshly, the family realises its selfishness, and Mrs Pearson learns to be firm.

learn.reallife: Workplace role-swap days in Indian companies, where managers do junior jobs for a day, rely on the same idea: experience teaches empathy.

learn.hook: No salary, no holidays, no thank-you. Priestley's comedy makes a serious point about the work that keeps families running.
points: Homemakers' work is often taken for granted; the play asks for respect and recognition.
Role reversal and self-assertion: standing up for yourself can change how others treat you.
Humour and satire on family life: Priestley mocks selfish habits through comedy.
Relevance today: in many families, unpaid home work, mostly done by women, is still undervalued; sharing chores and showing appreciation matter.

example.q: Is the play relevant to today's families?
steps: Home chores are still often done by one person.
The play's message about respect and sharing still applies.
example.answer: Yes: unequal, unappreciated housework still exists, so the play's message remains relevant.

learn.reallife: Campaigns in India encourage families to share housework, and many schools run 'help at home' projects. Priestley's message fits right in.

topics.title: How the humour works, and exam practice

learn.hook: Why is it funny when a mother drinks stout and scolds her husband? Because we never expect it. Comedy runs on surprise, contrast and exaggeration.
points: Humour comes from role reversal (meek mother turned bossy), contrast with expectation, exaggeration, dramatic irony and sharp comic dialogue.
The nickname 'Pompy-ompy Pearson' and the family's shocked faces add verbal and situational comedy.
Character sketches: Mrs Pearson (meek, then firm); Mrs Fitzgerald (bold catalyst); George (pompous); Doris (selfish); Cyril (careless).
Long answer: the dignity of homemakers and the need for respect; use incidents from before and after the swap.

example.answer: Mrs Fitzgerald is a bold, outspoken fortune-teller whose spell and firm behaviour make the Pearsons respect their mother.

learn.reallife: Indian sitcoms like 'Sarabhai vs Sarabhai' use the same comic tools: exaggerated characters, sharp lines and role clashes.
